instructions:
## Research objective

Your goal is to design modeling, simulation, and evaluation protocols that quantify the relative value of improving prediction versus expanding screening access to identify the worst-off (via the prediction-access ratio, PAR), and to reproduce the paper’s theoretical analyses and the German long-term unemployment case study.

## Plan Formulation

- Define the policy objective: maximize V(α, f; β) = Pr[screened | Y ≤ t(β)], where t(β) is the β-quantile of the welfare outcome Y and α is the screening capacity.
- Replicate two tracks: (A) theory-driven simulations under Gaussian and log-normal assumptions to compute V and PAR; (B) an empirical case study on long-term unemployment using administrative records.
- Operationalize the prediction-access ratio (PAR) as the relative gain in V from increasing α by Δα versus improving R2 by ΔR2; support both local (infinitesimal) and non-local (finite) improvements.
- Default parameter grids: α ∈ {0.01, 0.02, …, 0.50}, β ∈ {0.05, 0.15, 0.25}, R2 ∈ {0.0, 0.05, …, 0.95}, Δα, ΔR2 ∈ {0.01, 0.05, 0.10}.
- Key regimes to examine: scarce access (α ≪ β), moderate prediction (R2 ≈ 0.15–0.5), near-random prediction (R2 → 0), and near-perfect prediction (R2 → 1).
- Replicate figures: screening policy visualization (similar to Fig. 1), PAR surfaces (similar to Fig. 2, Fig. 7), PAR vs α for fixed R2 (Fig. 3), policy value curves (Fig. 4a), local improvement rates (Fig. 4b,c), capacity gap to match complex model (Fig. 5), and residual-based diagnostics (Fig. 10–15).
- Evaluate cost sensitivity: given a marginal cost ratio C_access/C_pred, present cost-adjusted recommendations using PAR; identify thresholds where expanding access dominates vs improving prediction.
- Plan optional fairness and robustness analyses: subgroup-specific PAR (e.g., demographics, regions), sensitivity to β and ΔR2 size, and uncertainty quantification via bootstrapping.
- Document assumptions explicitly: monotone screening rule on predicted outcomes ˆY, no harm from false positives, stable deployment distribution for evaluation; record any deviations.

## Data Preparation

- Theory track (no external data):
- - Gaussian model: Assume Y ~ N(μ, η^2). Generate ˆY so that (Y, ˆY) is bivariate normal with correlation ρ = sqrt(R2). Set μ=0, η=1 by default (location/scale shift does not affect ranks).
- - Log-normal extension: Let log Y ~ N(μ, η^2) and Y = ˆY · u with log u ~ N(0, γ^2); simulate ˆY and u to achieve target R2 on the log scale; use log transforms for evaluation.
- - Compute quantile thresholds on simulated samples: tˆY(α) = empirical α-quantile of ˆY; tY(β) = empirical β-quantile of Y.
- Empirical track (German long-term unemployment):
- - Data access: Obtain the FDZ SIAB-Regionalfile Scientific Use File (1975–2021). Respect all access, privacy, and use constraints; run all processing in the secure environment.
- - Cohort definition: Focus on unemployment spells beginning in 2010–2015 to allow 24-month outcome observation for duration Y (days), capped at 24 months.
- - Splits: There is a timeline inconsistency in the text; choose and document one of the two reproducible options:
-   Option A (as text states): train on starts in 2010–2011, validate on 2012, test on 2015 starts.
-   Option B (as figure suggests): train on 2010–2013, validate on 2012–2014, test on 2015–2017; ensure no leakage by computing outcomes only after full observation windows.
- - Feature construction: Follow Bach et al. (2023)-style covariates: demographics, labor market history, recent job details; aggregate to spell-level; handle categorical variables via one-hot encoding; target is unemployment duration in days (cap at 24 months).
- - Data cleaning: Drop records with inconsistent timestamps; impute or flag missing covariates; ensure consistent units; verify class prevalence for β values (e.g., LTU ≈ 12 months corresponds to β ≈ 0.15).
- - Normalization is optional (tree models are robust), but standardize for any linear baselines used in diagnostics.
- - Store derived artifacts: train/val/test indices, feature matrix, target vectors, feature metadata (categorical indices), and quantile statistics to guarantee reproducibility.
- Fallback synthetic dataset (if real data unavailable): Fit a log-normal to a reference unemployment duration distribution; generate features with realistic correlations; ensure the test Y distribution is right-skewed; provide seeds and generators to mimic β ≈ {0.05, 0.15, 0.25} cutoffs.

## Running Experiments

- Theory track computations:
- - Compute V(α, β, R2) using the bivariate normal CDF Φ2 with correlation ρ = sqrt(R2): V = Φ2(Φ^-1(α), Φ^-1(β); ρ)/β; use a high-accuracy numerical routine and guard against numeric instability at extreme α, β.
- - Local derivatives for sensitivity: ∂V/∂α via the univariate normal CDF formula; ∂V/∂R2 via the bivariate normal PDF formula; validate with finite-difference checks (±1e-5).
- - PAR for finite improvements: PAR(α,β;Δα,ΔR2) = [V(α+Δα)-V(α)] / [V(R2+ΔR2)-V(R2)] with Δα, ΔR2 in {0.01, 0.1}; compute across grids for α, β, R2.
- - Visuals:
-   • Screening policy curves: y ↦ Pr[ˆY ≤ tˆY(α) | Y=y] at fixed β and R2; show effect of increasing α or R2.
-   • PAR heatmaps over (α, R2) for fixed β; overlays for cost-adjusted thresholds (e.g., show contour where PAR = C_access/C_pred).
-   • Regions where V > 0.9 to highlight near-optimal allocation.
- Empirical track pipeline:
- - Baselines: Train CatBoost regressor (iterations=5000, early stopping=20 on validation; default depth/learning-rate unless tuned); also train a shallow Decision Tree (max_depth=4) as the simple comparator.
- - Evaluate out-of-sample R2 on the test set; expect a moderate baseline (≈0.15) in social prediction tasks; record random seeds and versions.
- - Policy value computation on test set: For each β, compute tY(β) on Y_test; for each α, compute tˆY(α) on predictions; V(α,β) = sum(1{ˆY ≤ tˆY(α)}·1{Y ≤ tY(β)}) / sum(1{Y ≤ tY(β)}).
- - Simulating improved prediction without retraining: Adjust predictions via residual scaling ˆY+ = ˆY + δ·(Y − ˆY), choosing δ to reach a target ΔR2; verify reduced residual variance and preserved residual shape.
- - PAR estimation (empirical): For chosen α, β, compute numerator V(α+Δα,β)−V(α,β); compute denominator using adjusted predictions to represent R2+ΔR2; assess Δ ∈ {0.01, 0.1}.
- - Special scenarios:
-   • Randomized screening (R2=0): replace predictions with noise or shuffled labels to simulate allocation at random.
-   • Near-perfect prediction (R2≈0.9): mix true Y with small noise or set ˆY close to Y while capping to avoid exact ties; examine behavior near α=β.
- - Capacity gap analysis: Compute minimal Δα* such that V_simple(α+Δα*,β)−V_simple(α,β) ≥ V_complex(α,β)−V_simple(α,β); interpret as additional screenings needed to match complex model gains.
- - Classification variant (optional): For fixed β define Y_cls = 1{Y ≥ F_Y(1−β)}; train probabilistic classifier; define policy 1{p̂ ≥ F_p̂(1−α)}; compare V curves to regression approach.
- - Subgroup and robustness analyses: Estimate V and PAR by subgroup (e.g., age, region, gender) to explore heterogeneous improvements; conduct bootstrap over test IDs to obtain CIs; perform sensitivity analysis over β and Δ values.
- - Efficiency and reproducibility: Vectorize quantile operations; cache V and PAR grids; parallelize over α-R2-β combinations; log all configs, seeds, and hashes of artifacts.

## Results Interpretation

- Confirm key qualitative patterns:
- - In scarce capacity regimes (α ≪ β), PAR grows large, indicating expanding screening access is more impactful than similar prediction improvements.
- - For moderate R2 (≈0.15–0.5) with α ≤ β, PAR ≥ 1 across broad regions, favoring capacity expansion.
- - Prediction improvements are most impactful in two regimes: first-mile (R2 → 0 with sufficient α) and last-mile (R2 → 1, especially near α = β).
- Quantify policy-relevant thresholds:
- - For β ≈ 0.15 (LTU ≈ 12 months), report the additional capacity Δα needed to reach coverage targets (e.g., 75% of at-risk identified); expect roughly stable Δα across β at higher α.
- - Provide cost-adjusted decision regions using the supplied C_access/C_pred ratio; highlight where access vs prediction is economically preferable.
- Compare models and operational choices:
- - Report the R2 and V gaps between the Decision Tree and CatBoost; contextualize whether increasing α by Δα* is cheaper than deploying the complex model.
- - Show where classification and regression formulations agree; note any deviations across α and β.
- Fairness and robustness takeaways:
- - Identify subgroups where prediction improvements yield uneven gains; if feasible, simulate targeted prediction improvements (e.g., reduce residuals for high-risk subgroups) and re-evaluate PAR.
- - Present bootstrap CIs for V and PAR surfaces; discuss numerical stability limits (e.g., extreme α, β).
- Limitations and assumptions:
- - Discuss assumption of no harm from false positives; note contexts where screening incurs costs or burdens.
- - Acknowledge administrative and operational costs (training, data integration) and how they shift cost ratios over time (fixed vs recurring).

## Report Writing

- Document the end-to-end setup: datasets, access constraints, cohort definitions, feature engineering, train/val/test splits, and preprocessing choices (with justification for any timeline choice).
- Methods: clearly define V(α,β), PAR(Δα,ΔR2), and the residual-scaling procedure to simulate ΔR2; include local derivative formulas and numerical validation steps.
- Models and training: list hyperparameters, early stopping criteria, seeds, software versions; include rationale for model choices and operational feasibility considerations.
- Results: provide tables and figures replicating key plots (policy value curves, PAR heatmaps, capacity gap Δα*, residual distributions), with uncertainty bands where applicable.
- Policy analysis: translate PAR and cost ratios into actionable guidance; show sensitivity to β, Δ, and cost assumptions; include scenarios for first-mile and last-mile improvements.
- Fairness and robustness: report subgroup analyses and any targeted-improvement simulations; discuss implications for equitable access.
- Ablations: compare regression vs classification, finite vs local improvements, Gaussian vs log-normal assumptions; note where conclusions are stable.
- Limitations, ethics, and governance: discuss risks from predictive profiling, transparency, auditability, and data governance; outline how to integrate oversight and periodic model updates.
- Reproducibility package: provide configuration files, seeds, and scripts to regenerate all figures and tables; include a checklist mapping scripts to figure numbers; note any non-public data with instructions for access or synthetic substitutes.
